prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and for developing it to the 1e-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from the topological insulators (B007) to the optical lattice clock. The deciding points are scientific, not the count of supporters. First, the two atomic physicists who know the field best, Eva Lindroth and Stefan Kroll, both put the clock first and answered my main worry. The 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy. It did not honour the idea that atoms in a lattice at the magic wavelength can be held without perturbing the clock transition, and it did not honour the 1e-18 regime that this idea opened. Second, the independent confirmation is of the kind I trust most: JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE have reproduced and surpassed one another, and the light-shift physics behind the magic wavelength is well understood by theory. Third, the clock has begun to yield physics: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tests of the constancy of constants, and dark-matter searches. Fourth, the credit chain of an originator of the concept (Katori) and the group that took it to the performance frontier (Ye) is short and was proposed identically by every member. That is a clearer attribution than I can offer for B007, where the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap stays open after round 1. I still think B007 is the deeper discovery of new quantum matter, and I would not oppose it in a later cycle.
statement.case_against: The clock remains, in the strict sense, an invention and a measurement capability. It builds on laser cooling (1997), the frequency comb (2005) and ion control (2012), and the surprises about nature that it may deliver have not yet arrived. Parallel contributions from Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups are real, and a two-name credit cannot cover them. The redefinition of the second has not happened. I am also a materials theorist and cannot judge the atomic-physics detail myself, so my move rests on the testimony of Lindroth, Kroll and Pearce and on the independent reproduction. Against my own earlier choice: I have not abandoned the view that topological insulators are the cleaner discovery of new physics, so a committee that weighs discovery over capability above all else could reasonably still choose B007.

responses.point: Lindroth argued that the 2005 comb prize did not address holding clock atoms in a lattice without perturbing the transition, nor the 1e-18 regime, and that the comb is the tool that makes a lattice clock readable and not the clock itself. She also invited my view on topological insulators.
responses.response: That argument is the main reason I changed position. My eighth place for B056 in the opening rested on the worry that the clock was a refinement of recognised precision spectroscopy, and your distinction between the readout tool and the clock concept answers it. On her invitation: I would say the topological insulator case is strong on physics and weaker on credit, because the HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang lies outside Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and the 3D confirmations by photoemission lie outside as well. I still disagree a little on the framing that the clock's attribution question is settled by eight identical proposals, since agreement among us does not remove the claims of Lemonde and Bloom. I do accept her point that a prize may name the originator of a concept and the group that took it furthest.

responses.point: Mehlig asked whether a citation restricted to the quantum spin Hall effect and its Z2 classification is defensible, or whether the wording must avoid implicitly claiming the 3D topological insulator story, which was established largely by photoemission groups outside the trio.
responses.response: My answer is that a quantum-spin-Hall citation is defensible on the science, since Kane-Mele and the HgTe transport are a coherent theory-plus-experiment pair. But it then leaves out the HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang that guided the experiment, and it cannot honestly cover the 3D materials or the ARPES confirmations that I cited in round 1 as the evidence for maturity. I conceded in round 1 that the trio is a deliberate cut through a larger field. After this round I do not see a wording that fixes both gaps within three names. That is why I no longer put B007 first, though I share your view that the physics is mature. I would be glad to keep it as the lead alternative for a later year.

responses.point: Danielsson called the topological insulators the strongest conceptual case on the list but said he sees no defensible solution to the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap, and that the 2016 prize means the committee must be sure this is a separate achievement.
responses.response: I agree with the first half and have now acted on it. On 2016 I still hold that time-reversal-invariant topological insulators are a distinct discovery from the topological phase transitions and Haldane physics honoured then. I am less sure than in round 1 that this distinction survives a hostile reading, and combined with the BHZ gap it makes B007 harder to defend this year than B056. Where I disagree with Danielsson is on his framing of the clock as the item with the cleanest attribution 'as anything on this list': the parallel strontium groups are a genuine omission, and I would want the citation worded around the lattice-clock concept and its performance frontier, not around precision timekeeping in general.

responses.point: Kroll argued that the performance is already confirmed by JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, that clock comparisons by fibre links are routine, that the clock opens new observation of nature, and that waiting for the redefinition of the second is not compelling.
responses.response: I accept the argument about independent confirmation, because it is the test I apply to every candidate. I also agree that waiting for the redefinition adds little. If the performance is reproduced across laboratories, the redefinition is an administrative consequence, not a precondition for the discovery. In the last round I said a redefinition would strengthen the case, and I now think that was too cautious. I would still ask him which results beyond accuracy he regards as the clearest physics output so far, since the redshift and constants tests are good measurements but not yet surprises. That bears on the citation, which I have worded around the invention and its performance, not around a discovery about nature.

responses.point: Pearce said that he and I are each outside our field on the other's first choice, and that if the committee cannot settle the B007 credit, the cleaner two-name clock prize is easier to defend.
responses.response: I agree with his symmetry point and with his practical conclusion, though not with the idea that defensibility alone should decide. What changed my view is that the atomic physicists answered the discovery-versus-capability objection with specifics (the lattice idea, the 1e-18 regime, independent reproduction) and that I could not close the BHZ gap in B007. I would not want the chair to read this as me following the majority. If the atomic members were to retract their view of independent confirmation, I would return to B007. Pearce's own request that the citation honour the lattice clock as a distinct invention is built into the wording above.

uncertainties: Whether the lattice clock is judged a discovery-level achievement or an invention and measurement capability; I defer to Lindroth and Kroll and cannot settle it from outside atomic physics.
Whether Katori and Ye are the fairest two names given Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and whether any citation wording can respect that.
Whether the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes weigh more against the clock than the atomic members suggest.
Whether B007 would be the better scientific choice if the committee could resolve the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit, which I think is unlikely within three names.
Whether the 2016 topology prize and the 2025 superconducting-circuits prize interact with B007 timing in a way I have underestimated.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My field is theoretical condensed-matter physics and electronic-structure theory, and I know the topological-materials community through spectroscopy-linked work, but I have no personal or institutional connection to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori or Ye, or to the other shortlisted candidates. I have been a member of the committee for several cycles, including as Chair for 2025, and the same conclusion holds as in round 1: no recusal is needed from my side. Moving from my own first choice in round 1 to B056 is a scientific judgment made after the discussion and is not driven by any link.
